title: Akyem Abuakwa: The Kingdom of Forest and Rivers

pages.text: Turn on a tap in Accra and fill a cup. Some of that water began its journey as rain on a range of forested hills about ninety kilometres to the north, near the town of Kyebi. Three rivers rise in those hills: the Densu, the Ayensu, and the Birim. Together they supply water to millions of people. The hills are called the Atewa Range, and they lie in the heart of an old kingdom, Akyem Abuakwa. Its king is the Okyenhene. The story of this kingdom is a story about holding on to a precious land.

pages.text: The Akyem are an Akan people. They formed three related states: Abuakwa, Kotoku, and Bosome. Abuakwa, the largest, built its capital at Kyebi, and its royal stool is named after an early king, Ofori Panin. The land was rich. Gold lay in the gravel of the Birim, and thick forest gave timber, game, and good soil. Cocoa later grew well here. But Akyem had powerful neighbours on both sides: Akwamu to the south-east, and later Asante to the north-west. To survive between them, the Akyem became known as stubborn and skilful fighters.

But Akyem had powerful neighbours on both sides: Akwamu to the south-east, and later Asante to the north-west.
To survive between them, the Akyem became known as stubborn and skilful fighters.
pages.alt: A royal stool on a platform inside a palace hall, with a state sword leaning beside it.

pages.text: For years Akwamu raided and bullied its neighbours. In 1730, the Akyem led an alliance that defeated Akwamu and drove its rulers across the Volta. Akyem Abuakwa gained wide new lands. The other struggle was harder. Asante wished to control the routes to the coast. Asante tradition says that in 1717 its first great king, Osei Tutu, was shot dead while crossing the River Pra during a war against the Akyem. Asante returned in 1742 and defeated them. The Akyem had to pay tribute for many years, but they never stopped resisting.

pages.text: In 1912, a new kind of king came to the stool. Nana Ofori Atta I had been to school and had worked as a clerk. He believed that the future of his people lay in education. During his reign of more than thirty years he opened schools, including a secondary school at Kyebi. He sat on the council that advised the British governor and argued there for the rights of chiefs and people. His brother, J. B. Danquah, became a lawyer and scholar. It was Danquah who helped to found the first political party of the independence movement, in 1947.

pages.text: The riches under the soil have been a blessing and a danger. Diamonds were found in the Birim valley in the 1920s, and gold is still mined. In recent years, illegal mining has torn up farms and turned stretches of the Birim brown. The forest on the Atewa hills is threatened as well, because the hills hold bauxite, the ore from which aluminium is made. Scientists have found plants and animals there that live nowhere else in the world. The people of Akyem face a hard question: how to gain from what lies under the land without destroying it.

pages.text: The Akyem have long said that the land belongs to the dead, the living, and the countless numbers not yet born. A chief does not own it. He looks after it for all three. That old idea fits exactly with what scientists now call sustainability: using resources in a way that leaves enough for those who come after us. Each year, at the Ohum festival, the people give thanks for the land and its rivers. When you next drink a cup of water, think of the hills where it started, and of who is looking after them.

activities.question: Why does the Atewa Range matter to people far from Kyebi?
options: Three rivers that supply water to millions rise there
It is the highest mountain in Africa
It is where cocoa was first grown

activities.question: What happened in 1730?
options: The British built a fort at Kyebi
An alliance led by the Akyem defeated Akwamu

activities.question: What is Nana Ofori Atta I best remembered for?
options: Promoting education and speaking for his people

activities.question: Apply it: A community is offered money to let its forest be cleared. Using the Akyem idea about land, what question should it ask first?
options: How quickly can the trees be cut?
What will be left for those not yet born?
Who will get the largest share today?

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from earliest to latest.
items: The Akyem build their capital at Kyebi
Osei Tutu is killed at the River Pra, according to tradition
The Akyem and their allies defeat Akwamu
Nana Ofori Atta I becomes king
